### Hitopadesha

-> 140 <-

If war has truly arrived, O King, why did you not prepare for it earlier? As it is said:

What kind of servant or minister is he who, at the very beginning, advises the King to engage in war or abandon his own post without careful consideration?

Furthermore:

One should strive to conquer enemies through means other than war. Victory is seen to be uncertain between two sides engaged in combat.

And again:

Through conciliation <term>sama</term> <gloss>peaceful negotiation</gloss>, gifts <term>dana</term> <gloss>bribery or tribute</gloss>, or sowing dissension <term>bheda</term> <gloss>creating division among enemies</gloss>—either used together or separately—one should strive to overcome the enemy, but never through war.

Moreover:

Every man is a hero until he has encountered battle. Who would not be full of pride before seeing the strength of the enemy?

What is more:

Success is not achieved by living beings through violent means as effectively as it is through small stratagems. These yield great results. However, seeing that war is imminent, let it be regarded with caution. For:

The <term>Chakravaka</term> <gloss>the ruddy sheldrake, appearing here as a wise bird counselor</gloss> says: O Great King, war should not be the first course of action. For what kind of servant or minister is he who, without reflection, advises the monarch to prepare for battle and abandon his own territory? Furthermore, one should try to conquer the enemy through conciliation and other diplomatic means, but never through battle. Between two combatants, it is not certain who will achieve victory. Furthermore, one should strive to resolve the conflict with the enemy through conciliation, gifts, or dissension—either separately or all together—but never through war. Additionally, all people are heroes when war has not yet occurred, because

<summary>A minister or counselor, identified as the Chakravaka bird, advises a king on the dangers of rushing into war. He emphasizes that diplomacy, including conciliation and bribery, is always preferable to the uncertain outcome of physical combat.</summary>
